For a pretraining researcher, the main takeaway is not a specific interpretability tool but a training lesson: if optimization consistently treats the transcript as the dominant signal, the model may preserve acoustic detail while still learning to suppress it during multimodal fusion.219:T851,作者先定义 teacher-forced prompt offset：对两段不同 prompt 接同一 continuation，逐 token 比较 hidden states 的差异。因为 continuation 相同，hidden state 差异可以视为 prompt 单独留下的 imprint。再定义 decodability ratio，把这个 imprint 的大小和不同 continuation 自身带来的 hidden-state spread 做比较，用来判断 prompt 信息是否还可读。

经验上，作者发现 offset 随生成步数 t 近似按 t^{-α} 衰减。训练后的 Pythia 模型在较深层通常 α≈0.55–0.7；未训练但架构相同的模型 α≈0.2–0.5，而且随深度增加反而更慢。这说明训练后的模型更快忘掉 prompt。与此同时，continuation spread 基本不增长，β≈0，因此 decodability 的衰减率和 imprint 本身几乎一致，可以用单一指数 α 概括遗忘速度。

理论部分给出一个条件 no-hair 定理。对有限深度 pre-LN Transformer，在 pre-norm 激活非退化等较弱条件下，prompt offset 的上界是 O(P(log t)^{L-1}/t)，prompt 对下一 token 分布的条件影响也以同阶消失。作者还构造了可精确求解的 uniform-attention 线性 relay 模型，证明 t^{-1} 上界是可达到的，而不是松的形式结果。

机制分析是全文最有意思的部分。作者把 attention 对 offset 的贡献拆成 direct path 和 relay path。direct path 是当前位置 query 直接读 prompt token；relay path 是当前位置读前面 continuation token，而这些 continuation token 自身已经携带 prompt 信息。随着生成继续，真正维持 prompt 影响的主要不是 direct read，而是 relay。训练过程压制的正是这条 relay 通路，因此遗忘速度加快。论文还指出，只看 attention 权重会误判，因为权重本身不能反映信息是否真的沿着 value/residual 路径被传递和保留。

在干预实验里，作者通过对 prompt 加 log t 级别的 logit bias 补偿均匀注意力稀释，发现可以部分消除甚至反转遗忘。这支持了“稀释 + relay 抑制”这一解释，而不是把遗忘简单归因于上下文太长。21a:T918,The central observable is the teacher-forced prompt offset. Take two different prompts followed by the same continuation, run the model under teacher forcing, and measure the hidden-state difference token by token. Because the continuation is identical, the difference isolates the residual effect of the prompt. The paper also defines a decodability ratio by comparing the imprint magnitude against the spread induced by varying continuations, which captures whether the prompt signal still stands out enough to be read off.

Empirically, the offset decays approximately as t^{-alpha}. In trained Pythia models, deeper layers typically show alpha around 0.55–0.7. In untrained models with the same architecture, alpha is smaller, around 0.2–0.5, and often decreases with depth, meaning slower forgetting. The continuation-induced spread is roughly flat, with beta near 0, so decodability decays at essentially the same rate as the imprint itself.

The theory section proves a conditional no-hair theorem. For finite-depth pre-LN transformers under mild non-degeneracy assumptions, the prompt offset is bounded by O(P(log t)^{L-1}/t), and the prompt’s conditional effect on the next-token distribution vanishes at the same rate. The authors also analyze an exactly solvable uniform-attention relay model, showing that the 1/t bound is asymptotically attainable.

The mechanism section is the strongest part of the paper. The attention contribution to the offset is decomposed into a direct path and a relay path. The direct path is the current query reading prompt tokens directly. The relay path is the current query reading continuation tokens that already carry prompt information. Long-range prompt influence is sustained mainly through relay, not through direct prompt reads. Training suppresses this relay channel, which explains why trained models forget faster. The paper further argues that attention weights alone are a poor diagnostic, because they do not tell you whether information is actually preserved through values and residual streams.

Finally, the intervention experiments add a log-t prompt bias to compensate for uniform-attention dilution. This can reduce or even reverse forgetting, supporting the dilution-plus-relay-suppression account rather than a vague “long context is hard” explanation.21b:T725,The experiments compare trained and random-initialized models under teacher forcing on coherent text. The headline numbers are: trained models in middle and deeper layers show forgetting exponents alpha around 0.55 to 0.7, while untrained models are around 0.2 to 0.5 and often forget more slowly at greater depth. The theoretical 1/t rate is an upper bound; real models usually decay more slowly but still follow a stable power law rather than an exponential. The continuation spread exponent beta is close to 0, except for untrained Qwen, so prompt decodability is governed mainly by imprint decay.

For mechanism validation, the direct-plus-relay decomposition reproduces the measured alpha within 0.06 across layers and training stages. That is a strong result: the decomposition is not just qualitative storytelling but quantitatively tracks the observed forgetting rate. In training dynamics, the paper finds that forgetting emerges within the first billion training tokens in Pythia, before attention sinks appear. This suggests prompt amnesia is an early training phenomenon rather than a late byproduct of a specific attention pattern.

The intervention section shows that mild log-t compensation improves instruction adherence, but with a small perplexity cost and a tendency toward instruction echoing. In multi-turn dialogue, adherence also trends upward, but the gain is not much larger than what one gets from a constant bias with the same mean. That implies the benefit comes mostly from allocating more attention to the instruction, not from any uniquely privileged shape of the log-t schedule.

The main empirical takeaways are threefold: prompt forgetting is approximately power-law, training speeds it up rather than slowing it down, and attention maps are not a reliable proxy for retained prompt information.21c:T440,This is a good skim paper, but it rewards careful reading of a few sections. The model input is formalized as x=(g,r,o,q): goal, record, observation, and typed question. The authors then build counterfactual paired states that independently vary the record, the observation, and an explicit success claim, allowing them to measure which source has more causal effect on commitment decisions such as stop, proceed, or buy. They evaluate on three domains: Android screen traces, ALFWorld, and WebShop, covering four decision models, seven open models, and their base LLMs. The main behavioral result is consistent across all 12 tested configurations: the record has a larger average effect on the decision than the observation, and after claimed-but-failed steps the models still commit in 53–100% of cases. To test whether the model internally knows better, they train linear probes on hidden states and find that step success is often decodable with AUROC 0.77–1.00 on held-out groups. Activation patching then localizes the mismatch: observation-derived information reaches the decision position by mid-depth, but record-dependent influence dominates in the final layers. The evaluation has two parts. First, they sample 200 prompts from each of five benign OR-Bench categories that are especially relevant to legal discourse: violence, sexual, harmful, illegal, and unethical. The main intervention is prompt prefixing. They compare no prefix, a lawyer prefix, a supreme-court prefix, and a jailbreak-style prefix. The legal prefixes are meant to reflect realistic workflow prompts rather than adversarial attacks. From the available full-text content, the paper includes the right controls for a study of this kind: local inference to avoid platform-level moderation, deterministic decoding, prefix robustness checks, and a jailbreak comparison condition. It would be useful to separate hard refusals, partial compliance with hedging, and safe-redirection behavior, and to report judge-human agreement more explicitly.223:T520,The paper introduces reasoning-aware multicalibration: keep externally important groups (e.g., topics that must be calibrated for policy reasons) and add internally important groups derived from observable CoT properties (uncertainty markers, revisions, self-checking, considering multiple answers, etc.). Then run a standard post-hoc multicalibration procedure (greedy iterative corrections such as iterative histogram binning) over the union of these groups.

A deliberate design choice is to use CoT signal as *group definitions* rather than as extra features for the base scorer:
- Calibration on topics is preserved by construction because the multicalibration constraints explicitly include them.
- The method is post-hoc: the generator and the initial scoring function are fixed, so it can wrap any existing confidence signal.
- Because calibrated scores are not used as rewards, the approach reduces incentives for CoT manipulation and is less sensitive to CoT unfaithfulness, as long as the observable properties remain statistically linked to errors.

The theory section formalizes when adding non-mandatory groups can reduce squared error, and identifies “internal importance” (groups that explain residual error beyond the mandatory groups) as a necessary condition—motivating CoT-based groups.224:T7a5,The model is a probabilistic context-free grammar defined on a fixed hierarchical tree. Sequences have fixed length over a discrete vocabulary, and the joint distribution is induced by hierarchical rules on the tree. Unlike experiments on neural LMs, the next-token conditional at each step is available exactly through belief propagation. This lets the authors cleanly separate the underlying language distribution from the decoding procedure: first compute the exact conditional, then apply a softmax temperature rescaling, and finally sample autoregressively.

The main observable is two-point mutual information. Because the hierarchical model is not translation invariant, the mutual information depends on absolute position as well as separation. The paper therefore focuses on the mutual information between the last token and the token located r positions earlier, which probes all hierarchical scales in a simple way. Across temperatures and grammar ensembles, the authors fit the decay of I(r) and test whether there is evidence for phenomena usually associated with criticality, such as a diverging correlation length, a transition from power-law behavior to a plateau, or a clear crossover to short-range exponential decay.

A notable part of the paper is the interpretation section. The authors give a tree-based statistical-mechanics view and an approximate mapping to an Ising model on a tree. This is used to explain why, in a fixed-tree hierarchical language, one should not expect finite-temperature correlation plateaus or the usual short-range exponential cutoff. Intuitively, the tree geometry itself induces multiscale dependence, while temperature mainly changes the strength of correlations and the fitted exponent rather than creating a sharp phase boundary. In that sense, the observed power-law behavior is better understood as a geometric consequence of hierarchical generation than as evidence of temperature-driven criticality.225:T67d,The experiments are numerical and deliberately clean. The focus is on correlation statistics, not task performance.

First, across the tested temperature range and multiple grammar ensembles, the two-point mutual information I(r) remains well described by a power-law envelope. Temperature changes the overall magnitude of correlations and also changes the fitted decay exponent, but there is no obvious special temperature at which the correlation structure changes qualitatively.

Second, this qualitative behavior is robust across different rule ensembles, although the detailed temperature response depends on the support structure and heterogeneity of the grammar rules. In other words, the exact exponent-versus-temperature curve varies with the grammar family, but the broader conclusion remains stable: power-law-like decay persists and no clear critical point appears.

Third, the Ising-on-tree analogy is used to interpret the numerical findings. In this finite-depth fixed-tree setting, the paper does not observe the standard signatures one would associate with true criticality, such as a diverging correlation length or a sharp phase transition. Therefore, changes in power-law exponents under temperature variation are not sufficient evidence for temperature-tuned critical behavior.

If you care about language statistics, long-range dependence, or decoding temperature effects, the figures and appendix are worth reading carefully.227:T471,The method runs the model twice: once on the original prompt and once on a reference where the source tokens are replaced by EOS, while the response tokens and target span remain fixed. The scalar objective is the summed log-probability of the target response span. DeltaTrace decomposes the finite difference in that score. Instead of ordinary backpropagation, it builds operator-specific finite-change rules and propagates effective secant slopes backward through the computation graph. A token’s signed attribution is the inner product between its embedding displacement and the propagated secant slope. Local conservation ensures that token contributions sum to the observed score difference, and that aggregating tokens into sentences or passages preserves the interpretation. The derivations cover attention products, normalization, and Gated DeltaNet-style recurrent memory, so the same attribution idea applies to both attention and linear-attention models. The implementation uses FlashAttention-like tiling and Flash Linear Attention chunking to keep auxiliary storage linear in sequence length at fixed width and chunk size.228:T6a7,The main contribution is the controlled experimental setup. The task is SECDED ECC memory-wrapper generation, chosen because it is finite, parameterized, and formally verifiable. For the widest design, the target length drops from about 44,237 tokens to 69 tokens, a roughly 640x compression.

They then compare seven training regimes: zero-shot, few-shot ICL, retrieval-augmented generation, LoRA SFT, full SFT, continued pretraining followed by SFT, and reinforcement learning from a formal verifier. This design is important because it separates representation choice from training recipe rather than conflating them.

A second technical strength is the leakage analysis. The encoder and decoder depend only on data width, so across 3,584 valid configurations there are only 8 distinct encoders and 8 distinct decoders. Random config-level splits therefore leak byte-identical substructures between train and test. The paper quantifies this and switches to width-disjoint splits, which is the right unit of generalization here.

Evaluation is also unusually rigorous. The oracle harness has five gates: lint, elaboration, self-checking simulation with exhaustive single-bit fault injection and random double-bit injection, formal equivalence against the reference, synthesis/PPA checks, and rejection of illegal configurations. That makes correctness decidable rather than estimated from a small handwritten testbench.229:T597,The empirical message is straightforward. First, output representation dominates training regime. As the target moves from long-form RTL toward compact configuration-level specifications, generation becomes much shorter, the error surface shrinks, and formal-equivalence rates rise sharply. On long representations, stronger training recipes help only modestly because the model still has to emit a large brittle artifact.

Second, naive data splits substantially overstate generalization. With width overlap, the train-test near-duplicate rate reaches 0.65–1.00 depending on the split, and the leakage worsens as corpus size grows. This is one of the most useful parts of the paper because it shows exactly how structural reuse can invalidate code-generation evaluation.

Third, once deployment cost is measured properly, compact-interface learning is far more efficient. A sub-50M model paired with the verified generator reaches 0.89 formal equivalence, while a 32B fine-tuned model reaches 1.00, but the smaller interface-learning setup uses about 1600x less inference energy per correct design. The point is not that small models beat large ones; it is that if a deterministic backend absorbs most of the implementation burden, model scale and training sophistication stop being the main bottlenecks.

The paper reports energy in joules per correct design, which is a much better deployment metric than raw pass rates alone.22a:T659,The paper has three technical components. First, it performs a broad empirical audit of patch-token decoding across many pretrained ViTs. For classification models, intermediate patch tokens are passed through the final classification head and scored by the true-class logit. For contrastive VLM encoders such as CLIP and SigLIP, patch tokens are passed through the image projection head and compared against a text embedding like “a photo of a C,” producing patch-level similarity maps. These maps are then evaluated by comparing scores inside the object region versus the background, allowing the authors to categorize models into aligned, inverted, or unexplainable regimes. Second, the paper runs controlled synthetic experiments where architecture is held fixed or nearly fixed while task structure, loss, data distribution, and training conditions are varied. The central finding is not that one factor deterministically controls explainability, but that these factors change the optimization bias: they alter which among multiple functionally valid solutions training is more likely to find. Third, the paper provides a theoretical toy construction. It defines a simple classification task and a single-layer transformer for which the optimal classifier can be implemented in infinitely many ways. Some of those parameterizations are aligned under token decoding, while others are inverted. This elevates the empirical observation into a structural statement: even when the implemented function is the same, zero-shot decoding maps can differ radically because internal representations are not uniquely identified.22b:T574,The experimental contribution is about breadth and consistency of the phenomenon rather than a single benchmark gain. The authors inspect dozens of pretrained ViTs spanning architectures, scales, and training objectives. The main empirical result is that aligned patch decoding is not universal. Many models exhibit inverted maps, and this is especially common in contrastive vision-language encoders such as CLIP and SigLIP, where object-region patches can systematically receive lower target-class scores than background patches. The controlled synthetic experiments then show that, for the same architecture, changing the task, loss, or data distribution can substantially shift the probability of converging to aligned versus inverted solutions. In other words, training conditions affect basin preference rather than enforcing a unique explainability regime. The paper also emphasizes that models with similar task performance can have very different patch-decoding behavior, supporting the claim that functionally equivalent solutions can induce different readout geometries. The provided full-text excerpt does not include complete tables or exact numeric values, so I cannot reliably report parameter counts, dataset sizes, or percentage deltas; however, the evidence clearly combines large-scale real-model auditing with controlled toy experiments, and both point to the same conclusion.22c:T9a6,方法设计很克制，核心是把“能力存在”与“组合后退化”严格分开。作者先从同一数据集抽取独立任务，要求模型在单题条件下已经答对，再把这些任务按固定模板直接串接成一个 prompt，形成大小为 k 的 composition。这样做避免了任务改写、提示变化、跨任务依赖等混杂因素，确保唯一变化是同一响应里要同时处理的任务数。随后按 task 级别计算 accuracy drop：比较某题在 k-way composition 中的正确率与 isolation 中的正确率差值，并用多次采样估计。

机制分析分两步。第一步是排除独立错误累积。若每题在 isolation 中失败概率为 p_i，那么组合后的退化若只是累积效应，per-task 正确率不应显著低于其单题水平；但作者观察到的 drop 明显更大，说明组合改变了每个子任务本身的求解过程。第二步是定位预算机制。作者统计模型在不同 composition size 下为每个任务实际生成的 reasoning token，发现随着 k 增大，平均每题 token 数系统性下降，并且近似 obey power-law scaling。这里的关键不是总输出长度触顶，而是在远未达到 context/output 上限时，模型仍然主动把每题“想”的篇幅压短。

在 fragile task 的定义上，作者不是凭任务类型先验划分，而是用经验退化模式来识别：某些题在不同随机采样、不同 composition size 下反复表现出更大 drop，这些题构成模型特定的 fragile 子集。全文进一步表明，这些 fragile 题在 isolation 中往往就有更长的 reasoning trace，说明它们更依赖充足的 test-time compute。值得注意的是，fragility 在同一模型内部相对稳定，但跨模型不完全一致，意味着这不是数据集固有难度，而是模型内部表征与推理策略共同决定的属性。

基于这个发现，作者提出 fragility-aware batching。它不改模型、不需要 logits 或内部状态，是纯黑盒策略：先通过经验测量估计任务 fragility，再按 fragility 把题分到不同 batch size。非 fragile 题放大 batch，让隐式预算自动压缩每题 token；fragile 题放小 batch，保留足够思考空间。它和常规“全都单独做”相比更省 token，和“全都大 batch”相比更稳。这个方法的意义不在算法复杂度，而在于它把一个认知层面的缺陷转成了可操作的 inference policy。22d:T977,The experimental design is the main strength. The authors separate capability existence from composition-induced degradation. They first select tasks that the model already solves correctly in isolation. They then leave those tasks unchanged and simply concatenate them into a single prompt using a fixed dataset-specific template. This removes confounds such as paraphrasing, task reformulation, or inter-task dependencies. The only manipulated variable is how many tasks share one response.

They measure task-level accuracy drop by comparing each task’s accuracy at composition size k against its isolated accuracy, using multiple trials for estimation. This lets them ask whether composition changes the model’s ability on the constituent task itself, not just the aggregate prompt success rate.

The mechanism analysis proceeds in two stages. First, they rule out independent error accumulation as a sufficient explanation. If each task merely retained its isolated failure probability, the observed per-task degradation should be much smaller than what they actually measure. Second, they analyze reasoning-token allocation. As k increases, the model systematically emits fewer reasoning tokens per task, and this reduction follows an approximate power law. The important point is that this happens even when the total response remains comfortably below the model’s explicit output limit, so the effect is not simple truncation.

They then define fragile tasks empirically rather than by task category. Some tasks repeatedly suffer larger drops across sampling noise and across composition sizes. These tasks also tend to have longer reasoning traces in isolation, which supports the interpretation that they are more sensitive to reduced test-time compute. Fragility is relatively stable within a model but differs across models, suggesting that it is not just dataset difficulty; it depends on the model’s internal representations and reasoning policy.

Based on this, the paper proposes fragility-aware batching. It is a black-box inference strategy: estimate task fragility empirically, batch non-fragile tasks more aggressively to exploit the model’s tendency to shorten reasoning, and keep fragile tasks in smaller batches so they retain enough budget. The contribution is modest algorithmically but strong conceptually: a weakness in budget allocation is converted into a practical scheduling policy.22e:T72f,The study spans eight datasets across mathematical and linguistic settings. Two are constructed by the authors: 1,000 indefinite integrals with symbolic verification, and OneWordQA, a factual QA set with single-word or numeric answers and minimal reasoning demand. The rest include established benchmarks such as GPQA-Diamond, GSM8K, and MATH-500. The model suite includes strong open-weight models as well as Claude Opus 5.

The first main result is that composition-induced degradation is robust. Even when only tasks solved correctly in isolation are used, per-task accuracy drops substantially as more tasks are concatenated, and the drop is much larger than what independent error accumulation would predict. This holds across both math-heavy and language-heavy datasets.

The second result is the token-allocation pattern. Reasoning tokens per task decrease systematically with composition size and approximately follow a power-law trend. Since the full response is still far from the model’s hard sequence limit, this is evidence for an internal budget-allocation behavior rather than explicit truncation.

The third result is the characterization of fragility. Tasks with longer isolated reasoning traces are more likely to be fragile under composition. Fragility is stable within a model across random trials and composition sizes, but the fragile subset is not the same across models.

The most actionable result is fragility-aware batching. Relative to solving every task separately, it reduces generated tokens by about 43% on average across datasets with no accuracy loss. The same idea transfers to a proprietary frontier model: on GPQA-Diamond with Claude Opus 5, generated tokens drop by 24% without degrading performance. That makes the paper relevant not only for evaluation but also for practical inference scheduling.22f:T574,Start with the problem setup in the introduction and the early part of Section 3. In the experiments, a base model is trained on ground-truth demonstrations, then wrapped with a scaffold to form a teacher. A same-class, same-size student is trained on the teacher’s traces, either from scratch or by fine-tuning the base model. The tasks include Dyck languages, Sokoban, and modular arithmetic. The scaffolds include verifier-guided backtracking, A* search with model-pruned expansions, and a simpler fixed-token-deletion regeneration rule. The key experimental design separates local competence from compositional competence: the base model can perform the local steps, while the scaffold maintains candidates, search frontiers, visited sets, or verifier-controlled backtracking state. The theoretical part models search through directed s-t reachability. The base model answers local edge queries, which are computable by constant-depth Boolean circuits. The scaffold repeatedly uses these local queries to run BFS and decide reachability. Internalizing the scaffold requires the student to decide reachability from the graph representation. Under standard precision assumptions, fixed-depth polynomial-size Transformers can be simulated by TC0 circuits, even with logarithmic-length chain-of-thought in the cited setting. Directed reachability gives the separation: the external harness computes a closure over local primitives that the restricted student model need not represent.233:T479,Across the controlled tasks, same-size students do not close the gap to the scaffolded teacher, especially out of distribution. The first is Iterative Orthogonal Subspace Decomposition. Instead of learning one linear probe, the method learns multiple orthogonal directions sequentially. After extracting one direction, it removes the already explained deceptive signal and searches for the next direction in the residual space. The goal is to capture complementary components of deception rather than redundant variants of the same feature. The second component is a Domain-Adaptive Gating Mechanism. Static combinations of these directions are not sufficient because a direction that is informative in one domain may be irrelevant or noisy in another. DDSN therefore uses a small amount of test-time few-shot adaptation to assign context-dependent weights to the extracted directions. In effect, the detector asks which deception components are active in the current domain, rather than whether one universal deception vector is present. Relative to standard single-direction probing, the key difference is not just moving from one dimension to k dimensions, but making the composition itself adaptive to context.235:T499,The main empirical claim is straightforward: single-direction probes can work within a dataset but generalize poorly across heterogeneous deception settings, supporting the paper’s argument that deception feature composition depends on context. DDSN achieves stronger and more stable performance across datasets. The headline numbers in the abstract are an average AUROC of 0.97 and 95% recall at 5% FPR with only 10 adaptation examples. The paper also claims that transfer across related domains can work without re-adaptation, and that the 10-example adaptation is only needed when there is a substantial context shift, which can be flagged by a lightweight classifier. The most important evidence, if supported in the full text, would be ablations on the number of subspace directions, comparisons across layers, tests against simpler multi-probe baselines such as PCA-style decompositions or static ensembles, and adaptation curves showing how much the gating mechanism buys over fixed combinations. The paper’s credibility depends less on the absolute numbers and more on whether the datasets are diverse enough to genuinely invalidate the single-direction assumption.236:Ta82,The setup is intentionally simple enough for mechanistic analysis. The task is to take K distinct integers, followed by a SEP token, and autoregressively output them in sorted order. Most experiments train at K=16 and evaluate across lengths from 2 up to N. The model is a two-layer, single-head, causally masked transformer with no positional encodings. Removing positional encodings is not just a simplification choice; it avoids a structural barrier to length generalization and prevents the model from relying on absolute-position-specific strategies.

The central finding is that training converges to two solution classes. One is effectively single-stage: the second attention layer can be ablated with little or no effect, so most of the sorting logic is implemented without meaningful second-layer participation. The other is genuinely two-stage: both layers matter, and ablating the second layer hurts performance. This second class generalizes almost perfectly to longer sequences.

The mechanistic analysis of the two-stage solution has two main components. First is cross-layer specialization. The two layers are not redundant; they appear to divide labor, especially on cases where adjacent sorted numbers have small gaps. The paper defines the gap as the difference between consecutive sorted elements and argues that small-gap cases are relatively rare at K=16 but become increasingly common as sequence length grows. A model that does not learn to handle these cases robustly can look perfect in-distribution and still fail under length extrapolation. Second is a hinting mechanism. The first layer appears to narrow the set of plausible next tokens or provide a structured intermediate signal, and the second layer then selects among these candidates. As the number of possible candidates grows with input length, this staged procedure is more stable than a flatter one-layer-style selection rule.

The paper also studies why one algorithm emerges instead of the other. A key result is that layer-wise initialization scale can strongly bias training toward the single-stage or two-stage solution. That matters because it shows the bifurcation is not merely a post hoc interpretability story; it is tied to controllable early training dynamics. The authors also test minimum-finding and a greedy coin denomination task. Minimum-finding shows the opposite pattern, where the simpler solution generalizes better, while the coin task exhibits a broader mix of behaviors. So the lesson is not that deeper or more complex solutions always generalize better, but that generalization depends on task structure, rare-pattern statistics, and whether layers learn complementary roles.237:T647,The experimental setup is compact but sufficient. The main configuration trains at K=16 with online sampling, batch size 4096, AdamW, learning rate 0.03, for 60,000 iterations. Models reach 100% training accuracy early and are then trained further to near-zero loss. Evaluation sweeps sequence length from 2 to N, with the main focus on extrapolation beyond the training length.

Three results matter most. First, different seeds reliably land in two mechanistically distinct solution classes under the same objective, and these classes are cleanly separated by second-layer attention ablation: one class barely uses the second layer, the other depends on it. Second, the gap in length generalization is large. The two-stage solutions remain nearly perfect beyond the training length, while the effectively single-stage solutions degrade substantially despite fitting the training length equally well. Third, the failure mode is tied to gap statistics: small-gap inputs become more frequent at longer lengths, and the two-stage solutions are more robust on exactly those cases. The excerpt provided does not include all tables and exact numbers, but the qualitative claim is strong: this is not a marginal improvement but a split between near-perfect extrapolation and systematic failure.

The most informative ablations are layer ablation, initialization-scale steering, and task transfer to minimum-finding and greedy coin denomination. The authors test whether the problem is crowding in busy directions and find instead that the digit-induced change is small. Random noise lands in similarly busy directions, while replacing the digit with a random word moves the state much more and is readable. For computed values, the paper proposes a stricter protocol: compare a candidate value against what input-copy traces allow, rank candidates under a prime modulus, check sign-flipped twins, and compare against answer mixtures and synthetic generic mixing. The setup uses a neutral prompt such as "{} is known for" and computes a linear readout at a fixed layer for entities of type t. Unlike an LRE, the entity lens does not use a relation template, does not use object supervision, and does not rely on subject-object pairs.

The paper studies two variants. The contrastive entity lens (CEL) uses differences between the target entity state and reference entity states, aiming to capture what is distinctive about the entity relative to others of the same type. The non-contrastive entity lens (NEL) drops that differencing because CEL turns out to be sensitive to the choice of reference set. For example, reference entities with different nationalities can artificially amplify or suppress nationality-related tokens.

The prediction target is not the gold object but LRE faithfulness: the rate at which the affine LRE decoder reproduces the model’s own top-1 prediction. The authors then ask whether entity-lens scores, computed without any relation information, can predict faithfulness across relations. They also run leave-one-type-out tests and controls for object cardinality and answer-token frequency to check whether the effect is merely driven by shallow dataset properties.

A useful additional contribution is methodological. The paper shifts part of the analysis from the relation level to the individual-fact level and argues that existing datasets contain artifacts that obscure progress, especially semantically weak first tokens and reference competition among plausible outputs.23b:T5aa,The proposed method is NR-SAE, a native-router sparse autoencoder. Each routed expert owns a small dictionary. When the frozen MoE router selects an expert for a token, the corresponding dictionary is opened; dictionaries for unselected experts are not scored. This differs from global SAEs over the summed MoE output and from approaches that learn a separate auxiliary router for the SAE.

The paper tests the factorization at two seams. In the reconstructive seam, the SAE receives a selected expert’s raw output yt,s and reconstructs it. In the predictive seam, a transcoder receives the common MoE input xt and predicts the selected expert’s output. The first setting tests whether expert outputs admit expert-local dictionaries; the second tests whether these dictionaries can capture the expert’s computation from its input.

The controls are carefully designed. Layout A is the native router-addressed design: 128 experts, each with a 512-feature bank; with eight routed experts per token, a token sees 4,096 candidates and selects 32 slots. Layout F matches A in total stored features and parameters but uses rank banks with many more candidates per bank. Layout B matches A in visible candidate count but groups by routing rank rather than expert identity. Layout R keeps A’s architecture but applies a per-sequence bijection from expert IDs to bank IDs, preserving grouping and capacity while destroying stable expert-bank identity.23c:T49f,The main checkpoint is Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, with 28 layers, hidden size 1536, vocabulary size 151,936, and 32,768 model position embeddings. Across Qwen, Gemma, and Llama checkpoints, realized layer order produces trajectories that are 1.60–2.24 times more aligned with the endpoint chord than endpoint-preserving shuffles. Trajectory-informed interventions also produce more target-specific changes in internal dominance endpoints than fixed or matched shuffled policies.23d:T791,The core idea is to identify cross-modal concept neurons. The authors adopt the key-value memory view of Transformer FFNs and treat individual FFN neurons as fine-grained units that can encode concept-selective directions. For a given label, such as angry, they run one forward pass with an audio example plus a question prompt, and another with a text description corresponding to the expected answer, such as “The speaker feels angry.” They then identify neurons that are strongly associated with that label on the audio side and on the text side, and measure their overlap.

If a shared subspace exists, matching audio-text label pairs should overlap in these label-relevant neurons more than mismatching pairs. This is the central departure from prior work that compares full hidden vectors using cosine similarity. The authors show that ambient-space similarity is dominated by dimensions unrelated to the label and therefore has weak discriminative value for concept alignment.

To move beyond correlation, they perform two causal interventions. First, they use steering: they shift activations along directions derived from text-side cross-modal neurons and test whether audio-based recognition moves toward the target label. Second, they deactivate the identified neurons by zeroing them out and check whether the target task degrades before unrelated tasks do. This makes the claim much stronger: text-defined internal directions can causally alter audio recognition, and the shared neurons are functionally necessary for at least part of the model’s cross-modal behavior.

Compared with earlier interpretability work, the paper is more specific in three ways. It does not just track where audio information flows across layers. It does not only identify audio-specific neurons. And it does not rely on probing alone. It asks whether audio and text meet in the same internal units, and tests that claim with interventions.23e:T73e,The study covers three LALMs: Qwen2.5-Omni, DeSTA2.5-Audio, and Audio Flamingo 3, across four attribute types: animal sound, emotion, gender, and spoken language. Several quantitative findings stand out.

First, cosine similarity between full hidden vectors is a poor signal for label matching. The authors report that label-independent dimensions account for 88% to 100% of its variance, which explains why matching and mismatching audio-text label pairs are barely separable in ambient space. This is an important negative result because it directly challenges a common way of arguing for multimodal alignment.

Second, in steering experiments, text-derived cross-modal neuron directions alter audio recognition much more effectively than random neuron sets. For Qwen2.5-Omni and Audio Flamingo 3, this holds for 35 of 48 labels; for DeSTA2.5-Audio, for 7 of 24 labels. A striking example is that Qwen2.5-Omni can be pushed to answer “happy” for silent inputs: the unsteered baseline is 20%, while the best random neuron set reaches 45%, and the targeted steering is substantially stronger.

Third, deactivating the cross-modal neurons damages the target attribute task before unrelated tasks. This pattern holds in all 8 task combinations for Qwen2.5-Omni and Audio Flamingo 3, and in 2 of 4 for DeSTA2.5-Audio. In Qwen2.5-Omni, deactivating only 0.2% to 0.7% of FFN neurons is enough to cause damage comparable to removing the most audio-specific neurons, even though the cross-modal neurons are less audio-specific. That suggests they occupy a bottleneck position for integrating acoustic attributes into the text-anchored semantic machinery.

The weaker effects in DeSTA2.5-Audio are plausibly explained by its use of ASR transcripts, which may let the model partially bypass the pure audio pathway and dilute the causal role of shared neurons.23f:T4eb,Start with the introduction and pay attention to the critique of cosine similarity. First, an ordinal granularity router predicts the appropriate disclosure level. The target is modeled as an ordered label space, such as A/B/C, ranging from abstention or very coarse disclosure to country/city level and then precise location disclosure. The router operates on a pre-generation hidden representation, typically the hidden state of the final prompt token at a chosen decoder layer. Using linear probing and ordinal regression, the paper shows that disclosure levels are recoverable and arranged along a common direction in representation space. This motivates projecting the hidden state onto a disclosure-granularity coordinate and routing it to a target level.

Second, a steering module applies route-specific hidden-state interventions during decoding so that the generated answer better matches the routed granularity. The framework is inference-time only: it does not require a separately fine-tuned model for each policy and does not depend on demonstration-heavy prompting. Compared with prompting, it acts more directly on internal generation dynamics; compared with training-based methods, it is cheaper to deploy and easier to adapt.

Technically, this is best understood as a representation-analysis-plus-activation-steering paper. The main novelty is treating contextual privacy as an ordered routing problem rather than a flat safe/unsafe classification task.241:T444,The experiments cover multiple VLM backbones. The first important result is the probing analysis: linear probes trained on pre-generation hidden states outperform the model’s raw responses on contextual disclosure alignment metrics. That shows the appropriate disclosure level is often encoded internally even when the model does not express it reliably.

The paper then demonstrates that disclosure levels exhibit an ordered structure along a shared representation direction, which supports the router design. In the main evaluation, the route-and-steer framework improves contextual disclosure alignment over unmodified models and baselines, while better balancing over-disclosure and under-disclosure and incurring only modest alignment tax. The method also generalizes to DoxBench, suggesting the intervention is not tied to a single benchmark distribution.

From a pretraining-oriented perspective, the main lesson is that internal representations and final behavior can be systematically mismatched. A recoverable signal in hidden states does not guarantee that the model will naturally use it during generation.243:T87e,The method has three main components. First is the definition and measurement of k*. Each task is cast as binary or one-vs-rest classification over frozen LM representations. A dense linear probe provides a reference AUROC C. The authors then search over subsets of representation coordinates and define k* as the smallest feature count whose best sparse probe recovers 95% of the dense probe’s performance above chance. The point is not to solve the optimal sparse selection problem exactly, but to use a fixed, reproducible protocol that supports comparisons across tasks and models. Second is cross-model feature correspondence. Similar k* values alone do not imply that models rely on similar features. To probe that, the paper uses sparse autoencoder features and compares the responses of selected task-relevant SAE features across models on shared inputs. The analysis controls for two easy confounds: label correlation and class-mean differences. On several tasks, selected features show stronger cross-model response correspondence than matched controls, suggesting some input-level alignment in the readout structure. Third is training intervention and downstream prediction. The paper compares base models with their instruction-tuned counterparts, and separately varies weights and input format to disentangle where changes in readout sparsity come from. Both matter, and the interaction is task-dependent. To isolate the role of target supervision, the authors run controlled synthetic experiments with binary factors. They create target aggregates paired with correct labels and control aggregates paired with random labels. Learned targets often admit single-feature readouts, while readable controls still require tens of features, even when controls share half their factors with a trained target. This supports the claim that supervision can compress a target into a direct linear direction without equivalently compressing related structure. Finally, k* is tested as a diagnostic for label requirements in student adaptation, for distinguishing head failure from representational loss after continual learning, and for understanding pruning sensitivity.244:T85c,The study evaluates 19 language models from five labs on 14 core tasks. Several results stand out. Second, on three tasks, selected SAE features show cross-model response correspondence beyond what is explained by matched label correlation, and this remains after removing class-mean differences. 6. 证据预算与 verifier：在两个语言模型 verifier 上，作者用“claim 需要多少 bits、evidence 提供多少 bits”的比较恢复了 Trace Budget adjudicator，区分支持证据与不足证据的 AUROC 达到 0.91。这里虽然不是预训练实验，但对 reasoning verifier 和 evidence sufficiency 分析有直接启发。247:T8b0,The core result is an exact decomposition of expected code-length gain from memory. For both context memory and fine-tuned weights, the expected savings split into three terms: (1) information stored about the query, (2) a prior-repair term that corrects the model’s output prior even when the memory does not directly encode query-specific evidence, and (3) decoding loss, which measures how much predictive value is left unused by the decoder given the stored memory. This decomposition is the paper’s main contribution because it cleanly separates what is stored from how well the model reads it out.

On the context side, the value of a context subset is defined by deleting that subset and rerunning the model, yielding an exact leave-one-out valuation for held-out queries. This only requires predictive probabilities and the ability to rerun with partial context, so it applies beyond transformers to occupancy networks, stereo networks, kriging-style learners, and TabPFN-like in-context tabular models.

On the weight side, fine-tuning is treated as writing information into a bounded parameter state. The paper derives capacity-based ceilings for what such a state can save. The decision logic is asymmetric but useful: if measured context gain exceeds the ceiling of any weight state with a given capacity, context is certified as the better channel; if a fine-tuned model exceeds the ceiling of any window-limited context memory, weights are certified as better. A particularly interesting result is that when the relevant evidence fits in context, fine-tuning can add at most the context decoder’s decoding loss. In other words, parameter updates only buy what the context pathway failed to decode, not arbitrary extra information.

The paper also introduces an anytime-valid test for the practical case where exact information terms are unavailable. It accumulates held-out evidence sequentially and controls error at any stopping time. The appendix goes further and writes a transformer KV cache exactly as a form of weight write with query-dependent addressing, which strengthens the claim that context state and parameter memory can be analyzed in one framework rather than merely compared by analogy.248:T95e,The experiments span language, vision, fluid dynamics, and tabular learning. The goal is not benchmark coverage but validation of the decomposition, certificates, and sequential test.

1. Certificate correctness: on a trained transformer, TabPFN, an occupancy network, and a stereo network, the paper reports 25 triggered certificates out of 64 possible cases in one setting and 36 out of 96 in another; every triggered certificate agrees with the empirically measured winner. The bounds are not always tight enough to decide, but when they do decide, they are reliable.

2. Choosing context vs weights with held-out tests: on two OpenML tabular tasks with 128 rows, the test selects TabPFN over XGBoost trained on the same 128 rows for every seed, indicating that in-context adaptation is the better channel in that low-data regime. On airfoil pressure fields, with 128 designs the test selects a trained surrogate over an in-context learner for every seed; when reduced to 32 designs, it switches to the in-context learner in two out of three seeds. This is a useful regime-dependent result: small evidence favors context, larger evidence favors parameterized learning.

3. Error control: on simulated streams with no true winner, the anytime-valid procedure incorrectly declares a winner on at most 3.3% of streams, below the nominal 5% level.

4. Local context valuation: in the occupancy network, 300 points that actually observe a local geometric feature contribute 17.66 bits per query, while 300 matched points from unchanged geometry contribute only 0.001 bits. In the stereo network, a camera that sees the queried surface carries about three times the bits of one that does not. These results show that the valuation tracks relevance, not just context size.

5. Non-monotonic context learning curves: in the occupancy example, one patch that covers the target feature reduces code length from 4.99 to 0.05 bits per site, while eight patches that miss the feature increase it to 9.06. More context can hurt when it is irrelevant or misleading. That observation is directly relevant to long-context modeling and retrieval-augmented systems.

Start with Section 3. That is the center of gravity. Focus on the definition of code-length saving, the three-term decomposition, and why the same law applies to both context and weights. Pay special attention to prior repair and decoding loss; those are what make the framework more informative than a plain mutual-information argument.

Then go to Section 5. This is where the theory becomes actionable: certificates, capacity ceilings, window ceilings, and the result that fine-tuning can only recover context decoding loss when the evidence fits in the window. For pretraining researchers, this section is the bridge to questions about parameter capacity, KV cache, retrieval, and continued pretraining.

Section 4 is worth reading for interpretability of the framework. The delete-and-rerun valuation is simple but revealing, especially in the occupancy and stereo examples where relevance and form are disentangled.

Section 6 is for the sequential testing story. The main point is not the task choice but how the anytime-valid procedure remains usable when exact information terms are unavailable.

If time is limited, read the Introduction, Section 3, and Section 5 first, then inspect one experimental domain you know well. That should take about an hour. If you want the strongest formal intuition for why ICL and fine-tuning are being unified, the appendix treatment of transformer cache as weight writing is worth careful study.24a:T8ac,The method has two complementary intervention paths: lesioning and steering.

In the lesion path, the authors first train an aphasia subtype classifier on clinical data from AphasiaBank. The classifier labels generated text as resembling different aphasia profiles, such as Broca-like or Wernicke-like behavior. They then systematically ablate attention heads in frozen LLMs and use the classifier to identify which ablations induce which subtype-like deficits. The key point is that the intervention is not evaluated only by generic quality drop, but by the type of linguistic impairment it produces. This lets the authors associate some language functions, such as grammatical fluency or semantic coherence, with relatively discrete structural circuits.

In the steering path, they compute subtype-specific intervention vectors from residual-stream activation differences between processing human aphasic transcripts and healthy-control transcripts. Adding these vectors at selected layers during generation pushes the intact model toward the corresponding aphasia profile. They also test whether subtracting such directions can partially reverse lesion-induced deficits. Conceptually, lesioning targets structural hardware, while steering targets representational state.

The most important result is not a simplistic localization story. The paper finds a dual picture: some language functions can indeed be induced or disrupted through relatively specific circuits and directions, but those functions are also strongly entangled. Different aphasia subtypes share substantial overlap in their lesion-sensitive components, and their steering vectors have high cosine similarity. So the internal organization looks neither cleanly modular nor uniformly diffuse. It looks like a densely distributed system with vulnerable critical substructures.

A notable design choice is the use of a clinically informed classifier as the main diagnostic interface instead of standard LM metrics. The benefit is a structured taxonomy of degradation types. The cost is dependence on the classifier’s training distribution, which the authors acknowledge and partly offset by showing stronger generalization for steering interventions.24b:T6e4,The experiments use AphasiaBank and focus on two elicitation tasks: Cinderella story retelling and sandwich-making instructions. These provide narrative and procedural speech settings with different linguistic demands. The model suite includes 11 LLMs from four families: GPT-2 XL, Llama-2-7B/13B-chat, Pythia 1B/1.4B/2.8B/6.9B, and Qwen3.5 0.8B/2B/4B/9B. Generation uses greedy decoding with a repetition penalty of 1.25 to avoid looping in base models.

The reported findings are mainly qualitative-structural rather than centered on one benchmark score. First, classifier-guided lesioning induces target aphasia-like subtypes more reliably than unguided or weaker intervention strategies, suggesting that some attention heads are more tightly linked to specific language failure modes. Second, steering can robustly induce corresponding aphasic behavior in intact models and appears to generalize better across tasks and prompts than structural lesioning. Third, there is substantial overlap across subtypes, both in the structural components implicated by lesioning and in the similarity of steering directions, supporting the paper’s dense-entanglement claim.

For a pretraining-oriented reader, the useful takeaway is that the authors turn language degradation into a structured, classifiable object and validate the pattern across multiple model families and scales. That said, the scope is limited. The study focuses mainly on attention-head ablations and residual-stream steering, not MLP circuits, multi-component pathways, or training-stage evolution. The clinical classifier may also conflate some stylistic distortions with aphasia-like deficits. So the results are better read as mechanistic probes than as strong evidence of cognitive equivalence.24c:T514,Start with the introduction and method. The key framing is that aphasia is used as a taxonomy for LLM failure modes, not as a medical application. Then read the data/setup section to understand why AphasiaBank and the two elicitation tasks were chosen, and how prompts and decoding were standardized across model families.

The most important results to inspect are the classifier-guided lesion findings and the steering experiments, especially any evidence for induction and partial reversal of subtype-like behavior. If the full paper includes ablations, the most important ones to inspect are the removal of progress signals, verifier gating, and cross-window training support.250:T49e,The framework is called Harness-Policy Optimization (HPO). A coding agent is modeled as a pair of policy P and harness H, with trajectories scored by an executable verifier. Each round alternates two updates. In the H-step, the current policy is frozen and used to analyze its own failed trajectories, propose harness revisions, and select the best candidate on a search set. The harness can modify prompts, context organization, tool usage flow, feedback format, and stopping rules. In the P-step, the selected harness is frozen and the policy is updated with reinforcement learning under that harness. The updated policy then becomes the proposer for the next H-step. Crucially, the harness search set is also updated using hard tasks identified during the preceding policy-learning phase, so harness search stays aligned with the policy’s current weaknesses. The paper instantiates two versions: Self-HPO, where the evolving policy proposes its own harness candidates, and an external-model variant using Opus 4.8 as a fixed proposer. The main design insight is not merely “optimize both,” but to couple proposer identity and search-set construction to the evolving policy.251:T410,The base policy is Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and the seed harness is mini-SWE-agent. A deeper read is only necessary if you want to port the idea beyond coding agents, in which case the definition of the harness search space becomes the key detail.253:T6b4,The method starts with diagnosis. A behavioral checker replays successful trajectories, tracks repository state and required checks, and labels actions that go beyond what the task requires. The first such action in a successful run is treated as the onset of over-defense. By resampling from the same prefix, the paper shows that these points are silent forks: the next action can vary in proportionality while preserving success.

The paper then explains why a straightforward RL fix is weak. One can add checker-based penalties to the trajectory reward, similar in spirit to length-controlled RL. But that signal reaches a given fork only through trajectories that remain proportionate at all relevant forks. As trajectories get longer, such fully proportionate rollouts become rare. Under GRPO, which updates from within-group reward differences, many rollout groups become reward-identical, so the policy receives little or no learning signal.

The proposed solution is ForkDPO, a fork-level preference optimization scheme. Instead of inferring credit from outcome, it directly constructs preference pairs at the behaviorally meaningful fork. There are two pair types. One targets over-defense: the checker identifies the first disproportionate action in a successful trajectory, and the model is resampled from the same prefix to obtain a more proportionate alternative. The other targets under-checking: when immediate submission would skip a required check, the method also creates pairs on that side, so the model does not simply learn to check less. DPO is then applied to these fork-level pairs. The key difference from random-turn DPO is precise signal placement at the actual behavioral branching point.254:T618,The empirical story has three parts. First, the diagnosis: on a 4B model and four frontier models, silent forks are shown to be where over-defense begins. Under implicit budgets, when models are prompted from these fork prefixes, they choose the disproportionate branch in up to 91% of decisive actions such as testing, checking, or submitting. The paper also notes that both branches usually leave the repository unchanged and that over-defensive runs succeed as often as other runs, which directly supports the claim that outcome does not distinguish behavior quality here.

Second, the failure of reward-based fixes: when the checker is folded into the trajectory reward and training is done with GRPO, 71% to 74% of rollout groups under implicit-budget settings receive identical rewards, so relative updates largely vanish. After 12 rounds, the disproportion rate does not meaningfully improve. Random-turn DPO also helps little, indicating that the issue is not merely the absence of preference data, but the location of that data.

Third, ForkDPO improves behavior on 48 test tasks from unseen repositories. For the 4B model, the implicit-budget disproportion rate drops from 70.3% to 58.9%, an 11.4-point reduction. Median runtime falls from 143 seconds to 90 seconds, roughly a 37% decrease. Random-turn DPO only reaches 67.7%. The ablations also argue that both sides of the behavior boundary matter: penalizing over-defense alone can push the model toward insufficient checking, while adding pairs for required checks stabilizes the target behavior.255:T52b,Start with the introduction and the first motivating figure. 第二层是 PRPO，Peer-Relative Policy Optimization。每一侧不是单个 policy，而是 N 个 LoRA adapter 组成的同角色种群，挂在同一个 frozen base 上，LoRA 参数量约为基座的 0.1%，便于低成本维护多策略与权重重组。每一轮固定一个条件 ω=(scenario, frozen opponent committee, decoding budget)，让同角色策略在相同条件下比较。作者把 same-role peers 放进 advantage baseline，而不是放进 opponent pool、reward shaping 或 learned critic。直观上，这样做的目的是让某个 policy 的得分反映“在同样对手、同样任务、同样预算下，它比同伴好多少”，从而把对手强弱波动和样本难度波动从梯度信号里扣掉。文章把这种收益称为 matched-population advantage，并给出 advantage variance 的闭式分析。为避免种群退化，训练中还有 tournament 机制：淘汰最弱 adapter，并从较强策略重播种，维持策略多样性。

还有一个设计值得注意：这是非零和游戏。Red 不能靠生成无法构建或无法通过测试的垃圾补丁来“骗赢”，因为 reward 由执行验证决定，必须同时满足功能正确与 exploit 可达。这个约束很关键，它把攻击者从“让 Blue 犯错”改成“生成真实、可部署、难检测的危险改动”，使训练信号更接近实际代码代理场景。257:T8a4,The method has two layers. The first is an execution-verified training environment. The authors instrument known weakness classes into containerized copies of real repositories and only admit a site if an existing exploit harness can actually fire. This yields samples with executable ground truth: not merely that a vulnerability class is present, but that there exists a reachable exploit path. Red edits a reference diff that already completes a development task and passes tests. On vulnerable scenarios, Red must introduce one reachable weakness of the target class while preserving functionality. On clean scenarios, Red makes a similarly sized edit that introduces no weakness. Blue acts as an LLM code reviewer: it must classify the patch and localize the entry point, critical operation, and trace, which makes the output actionable rather than purely binary.

The second layer is PRPO, Peer-Relative Policy Optimization. Each side is a population of LoRA adapters over one frozen base model, with adapter size around 0.1% of the base parameters. A training round fixes a condition consisting of the scenario, a frozen committee of opposing policies, and a decoding budget. Same-role policies are then compared under identical conditions. The key idea is to place the population inside the policy-gradient baseline rather than in the opponent pool, reward shaping, or a learned critic. Intuitively, a policy is rewarded for outperforming peers that faced the same task, same opponents, and same budget, which removes some variance due to opponent strength and instance difficulty. The paper calls this the matched-population advantage and provides a closed-form analysis of the resulting advantage variance. To avoid strategic collapse, the population is maintained with a tournament mechanism that retires weak adapters and reseeds them from stronger ones.

An important design choice is that the game is non-zero-sum. Red cannot win by producing broken code that fails to build or fails tests. Rewards are execution-verified, so Red must generate patches that are functional, exploitable, and difficult for Blue to detect. That makes the training signal much closer to realistic code-agent deployment.258:T69a,The experimental program is organized around five questions: whether the attacker is reliable enough to train against, whether co-evolution beats static training, whether the detector transfers to unseen applications and languages, whether weight updates are necessary, and whether a population helps under a fixed verifier budget. - Asynchronous architecture: on a single 8×B200 node, 2 GPUs train the policy while 6 GPUs run independent vLLM inference engines that keep generating rollouts while training proceeds. Weights are refreshed after every update, so a single multi-turn trajectory can span multiple policy versions.
- Off-policy control: a max_off_policy_steps threshold bounds policy staleness; rollouts exceeding it are dropped.
- Consistency constraints: align training and inference engines (tokenization, numerical/logprob paths) and maintain consistent cached state across policy updates to prevent importance ratios from being corrupted by implementation mismatch.

The paper also shows a useful counterexample: Claude Opus 5 has the highest AUC on Verified/Sonnet but raises cost per solve by roughly one third because monitoring is too expensive.25c:T58f,REM (Reusable Experience Memory) introduces three explicit decisions, executed from within the agent’s loop:
1) What to store:
- Each completed run is a 55K–170K token trajectory with heavy exploration noise.
- REM consolidates it into a phase-structured document organized by four phases: localize, understand, fix, verify. This document is both the retrieval unit and the primary injected context, avoiding duplicated token spending.
- The design choice is deliberate: not raw trajectories (too noisy and context-hungry), not atomized factoids (lose solution structure).
2) When to recall:
- Two-tier read path: the phase document is injected at task start; a much costlier “implementation record” (fine-grained details closer to the original trace) is withheld.
- A struggle-gated in-loop node injects the implementation record only when the running agent appears stuck, leveraging the fact that the agent state is observable only inside the loop.
3) What to forget:
- The implementation record is evicted after a single exposure (one-shot eviction) to prevent persistent bias; the phase document remains for the whole run.

Ablations are framed to show gains come mainly from the stored form, while gating/eviction prevent the second tier from causing harm.25d:T406,AscendEvolve couples platform knowledge with evolutionary kernel search. The system has three main design choices. First, it builds a hierarchical and version-aware corpus from documentation, headers, and vendor operator libraries, then distills it into per-operator evidence before search. This avoids repeatedly processing a large heterogeneous corpus. Second, it uses demand-driven retrieval: concrete implementation or optimization questions are routed to a small set of relevant sources instead of placing broad documentation into the prompt. Third, it creates bidirectional interaction between retrieved knowledge and execution experience. Retrieved mechanisms seed candidate implementations; compilation, execution, and profiling provide empirical verdicts on the evidence used; these verdicts influence later retrieval and search. The evolutionary search maintains multiple mechanism-distinct implementation lines, so the agent can explore different implementation families rather than prematurely committing to one route.25e:T616,The method has a data side and a training side. The data side is called Refine. Starting from simple multimodal questions and successful candidate reasoning chains, it extracts an entity chain and then applies three controllable operators. Expand appends L evidence-supported hops after the original chain, turning the original answer into an intermediate node and forcing the agent to continue searching. Blur selects M internal nodes and attaches W retrievable but indirect facts to each, replacing explicit entity mentions with searchable clues and increasing disambiguation difficulty. Visualize selects N nodes near the end of the chain, retains up to P retrieved images per node, and injects visual evidence requirements so that solving the task requires both textual and visual retrieval. The pipeline also includes validation and filtering to reduce shortcuts from parametric knowledge or alternative evidence paths. On the training side, the paper uses joint RL and OPD. RL uses answer rewards plus lightweight behavior penalties to discourage redundant verification and premature stopping. OPD is not applied as full-trajectory hard distillation; instead, token-level teacher guidance is applied on the student’s own imperfect rollouts, with strength modulated by a shaped reward gap, and the OPD coefficient is exponentially annealed over training. The motivation is clear: pure RL gives only a coarse scalar signal, while full distillation can overwrite exploration with teacher behavior. The proposed scheme tries to keep the benefits of both.25f:T405,The main evaluation uses synthetic financial transaction QA. The inner loop roughly triples coverage across 13 starting operator sets. Mistral-Small-24B and Llama-3.3-70B show comparable self-extension, with yield tracking each model’s fluency in the DSL.260:T7a1,FedSkillGit is explicitly inspired by Git-style incremental collaboration. The server maintains a shared skill document d and a global experience document e. Each client has private train/validation splits and four LLM-based roles: an executor for task execution, a skill optimizer for local refinement, a sanitizer for privacy cleaning, and an auditor for private-value checking. Instead of uploading a rewritten full skill document, the client generates semantic commits: localized skill patches together with supporting experience summaries.

The pipeline has several stages. First, local skill evolution: the client executes tasks using the current global skill and global experience context, collects local successes and failures, and asks the optimizer to produce revisions. Second, two-stage privacy filtering: a sanitizer rewrites or removes sensitive content, and an auditor checks whether the commit still contains private values or environment-specific details. This is not formal differential privacy; it is semantic privacy filtering performed by LLM agents. Third, cross-round experience reuse: the server maintains a global experience document that accumulates reusable evidence over rounds and redistributes it to clients, reducing redundant rediscovery and making local optimization more informed. Fourth, experience-aware aggregation: the server uses a merge agent to combine commits with reference to the global experience document, rather than simply concatenating or voting over full documents. Fifth, version validation: a candidate updated skill is only published if it passes validation.

Relative to straightforward federated baselines, the key differences are the shift from document-level to commit-level updates, the inclusion of evidence alongside edits, and the explicit use of a shared experience memory. That makes the system closer to collaborative knowledge editing with validation than to standard federated averaging.261:T63a,The paper reports experiments on three datasets and three LM families. The headline result is that FedSkillGit outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 22% and approaches centralized performance. From the provided full-text excerpt, the most reliable takeaways are as follows.

First, overall effectiveness: the gains appear across multiple datasets and backbones, suggesting that the improvement is not tied to a single model family or task distribution. The paper positions the method against federated baselines that evolve and aggregate full skill documents, and the reported gap indicates that the update representation itself matters.

Second, communication and privacy motivation: because the method transmits semantic commits rather than full documents, the communication cost should scale with newly acquired knowledge instead of accumulated skill length. When reading the full paper, the most important tables and plots to verify are communication curves, average commit size, and how document growth behaves over rounds.

Third, ablations: the architecture strongly suggests useful ablations around removing privacy filtering, removing the global experience document, disabling version validation, and replacing commit-level aggregation with full-document aggregation. Those ablations are likely where the paper justifies why each component exists.

The excerpt provided here does not include the full experimental tables, exact model sizes, or dataset sizes, so precise numbers beyond the reported “up to 22%” should be checked directly in the original paper before citation.262:T46d,LEASH formulates weak-to-strong escalation as a budget-constrained sequential stopping problem, where the weak model’s estimated failure risk acts as a proxy for the benefit of escalation. It builds a representation bank from a small set of held-out tasks by recording hidden states on prompt and action tokens and labeling them with task-level and subgoal-level outcomes. At test time, the current prompt or execution trace is scored by a Mahalanobis-distance criterion: the hidden state is uncertain if it lies closer to past failures than to past successes. This score drives two mechanisms. First, an initial gate decides whether to escalate at the start, while a runtime gate monitors the weak agent during execution. Second, after handoff, the weak model becomes a shadow observer for the strong model, checking the trajectory every three steps. If uncertainty is high, the pending action is rolled back and re-decided once with higher reasoning effort. The main difference from prior escalation schemes is that no additional monitor training, external knowledge base, reference model, or per-step multi-sampling is required.263:T80b,The framework is a sequential-auction MDP. A task is modeled as a finite-horizon MDP, but actions are not chosen by one global policy. Instead, a society of agents bids for the right to act on the current state. The winning agent transforms the state and then resells the resulting state into the next auction. When the task reaches a terminal solution, the final reward is propagated backward through the resale prices, implementing a bucket-brigade style temporal credit assignment.

The starting point is the theory of Chang et al., where Vickrey auctions align local bidding incentives with the globally optimal MDP policy under perfect competition. The paper argues that this assumption is economically unrealistic for LLM societies. With exact clones, the winner pays essentially its true valuation, so expected profit goes to zero and participation becomes irrational. At the other extreme, if an agent is the only eligible buyer at some step, it behaves as a monopsonist and bids the minimum needed to win. The clearing price collapses, upstream contributors are underpaid, and the multi-step chain becomes unsustainable.

The proposed shift is to study imperfect competition. Agents are similar enough to compete, but differentiated by inference cost, prompting, heuristics, and capability. Since LLMs are poor zero-shot estimators of their own success probabilities and token costs, the paper does not rely on direct self-evaluation. Instead, each agent learns a lightweight valuation policy with reinforcement learning to decide whether to bid and how much to shade its bid. The paper benchmarks four bidding strategies: Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO. It also compares multiple auction rules, including first-price, second-price, and a credit-conserving Vickrey variant.

Methodologically, the contribution is less about one new algorithm and more about building an experimental framework that combines sequential auctions, LLM agents, learned valuation policies, and market-density analysis under imperfect competition.264:T4ed,The experiments have two roles. One is to validate the economic failure mode: in synthetic settings, the authors show monopsony failure, where lack of competition collapses bids and prevents value from flowing upstream. The other is to test whether realistic intermediate regimes work: they run market-density sweeps and compare decentralized markets against centralized orchestration baselines on task success and agent profit.

The domains mentioned in the paper include math reasoning and a newly constructed synthetic news market. The main empirical conclusion is that no competition fails, but perfect clones are not required either. A middle regime of imperfect competition is sufficient to sustain positive profits while also achieving higher task success than centralized orchestration baselines. That is the main result to retain.

That last point matters, because accuracy alone would miss whether the market is economically viable.265:T659,The proposed method, SchemaShield-Lite, is a training-free inference-time robustness layer with three components. First, each tool is rendered into a compact canonical card containing the tool name, description, required fields, and field-level type information. This normalizes presentation and emphasizes the current schema. Second, after the base model emits a tool call, a validator checks the tool name, required fields, and argument structure, returning structured error information rather than a binary valid/invalid flag. Third, if the call is invalid, the model is prompted again with the task context, the canonical tool card, the invalid call, and the validator errors, and asked to repair the output. Under the primary non-oracle protocol, repair is staged. If the base call already names a visible tool, the system performs constrained repair against that tool. If the tool name is missing, it first runs a candidate-set retry over visible tools to resolve a concrete target, then performs tool-constrained repair. The paper highlights three implementation details that materially affect results: the repair prompt must explicitly ask the model to infer all required fields from dialogue context; candidate-set retry is necessary when the tool name is absent; and the repair stage needs a larger token budget, raised to 512 tokens in their setup to avoid truncation on longer examples.
